about: I finished an M.S. in aerospace engineering at Georgia Tech in May 2026, in the BS/MS honors program. The B.S. was there too, in three years, in May 2025. Undergraduate GPA was 4.0.

Before that I interned at Johns Hopkins APL in Summer 2025, on error-state Kalman filters and robust flight control. I also did undergraduate research in the Dynamics and Control Systems Lab, and I led avionics and controls for the Ramblin' Rocket Club for two years.
I live in Los Angeles. I'm originally from Annandale, Virginia, and I went to school in Atlanta. I'm an Eagle Scout, July 2020. I play tennis, run, lift, and read.

projects.title: Jet vanes rocket
projects.summary: State estimation and an LQR flight controller for a rocket steered by jet vanes in the motor plume. I led the avionics, the C flight code, and GNCSIM.
projects.vizLabel: Jet vane pitch loop, with a 5 degree reference that then returns to vertical.

sections.heading: What We Were Building
paragraphs: Jet vanes are small diamond-shaped vanes in the exhaust of a solid motor. Deflect them and you get a side force. As far as I know, a collegiate team had not flown this before. I led the electrical, software, and flight-dynamics side of the GNC project in the Ramblin' Rocket Club from 2023 to 2025.
We started the jet vanes rocket in February 2024.

sections.heading: GNCSIM
paragraphs: To design the controller I needed a 6-DOF simulation I could change quickly. GNCSIM is that package: environment, rocket, aerodynamics, and flight as classes, and one master file where you set the case and run it. The Flight class integrates with RK4 and writes the plots. A Monte Carlo class puts uncertainty on thrust, mass, center of gravity, aero, and wind.
The equations live in one model function. It returns the derivatives of position, velocity, attitude, and attitude rate given the state, the environment, and the control.

sections.heading: LQR Along a Nominal Flight
paragraphs: LQR is the controller because it lives in the time domain and it is multi-input, multi-output. The command is u = −Kx. Q weights how hard you chase the state. R weights how hard you work the actuators. The rocket is not linear, and thrust, aero, and density all change, so I linearize at breakpoints taken from an open-loop nominal run. At each breakpoint, K = lqr(A, B, Q, R) in MATLAB, and in flight you pick the breakpoint closest to the current state.

The control vector is a desired moment, not a vane angle. That let us finish the controller before the actuator model was settled. Moment becomes side force from the center of gravity, and side force becomes a vane deflection once the static fires gave us that map.

Closed loop, the rocket goes up, yaws to about 5°, and straightens. Monte Carlo with the gain matrices from a slightly different vehicle still behaved, so we treated the controller as verified in simulation.

sections.heading: Navigation
paragraphs: Position and velocity use an extended Kalman filter. Predict integrates the accelerometers. Update takes GPS. Aero is hard to trust, so the predict step does not fly a full dynamics model. GPS loses lock under high-g, and when it does the filter skips the update and lets the covariance grow until lock comes back.

Attitude is a quaternion propagator on the gyro. There isn't a reference sensor accurate enough to correct it: a magnetometer is off by degrees, which is too coarse here. Given the sensors and how short the flight is, the integrated gyro drift was small enough to live with.
On the pad, a separate ground filter estimates accelerometer and gyro biases. The vehicle is sitting still, so a nonzero mean is bias. It has to converge before we arm the flight filter.

The state machine is Idle, Ground, Fast Ascent, Slow Ascent, Freefall, Landed. We flew the estimation on the avionics test rocket in November 2024. Bad GPS updates pulled the position estimate around. The attitude propagator did its job. That is the structure we built for the jet vanes rocket.

sections.heading: Hardware and Static Fires
paragraphs: Sensors are an ADIS16500 IMU and a u-blox GPS, on a board we called Vaney: two STM32s, an XBee, flash, an SD card. Power comes from a separate board that bucks a 4S LiPo down to 3.3 V, 5 V, and 8.4 V for the servos, and it holds the pyro channels. One microcontroller estimates state. The other runs the control law, the servos, telemetry, and logging. The C follows NASA safety-critical coding rules.

April 2024 we static fired for a nominal thrust curve. The vane mount failed. October 2024 we fired a yaw sweep. The tungsten-copper vanes eroded, so the team moved to pure tungsten. I built the avionics for those tests: an XBee and an Arduino that fire the motor from a safe distance and then run an open-loop servo sweep. The notes from August 2025 still listed a third static fire, to confirm the tungsten and the deflection-to-side-force curve.

projects.title: Autonomous racecar
projects.summary: MPPI for Georgia Tech's F1Tenth cars. The controller does not need the track in advance. It builds a centerline from LiDAR and picks a lowest-cost rollout.
projects.vizLabel: Sampled MPPI rollouts on an oval track, lowest cost in green.

sections.heading: The Idea
paragraphs: The lab's F1Tenth cars are small vehicles for small-scale racing. I was asked to put Model-Predictive Path Integral control on one. You sample steering and acceleration, roll a kinematic bicycle model forward, and keep the trajectory with the lowest cost. Most racing controllers want the track ahead of time. This loop does not. It will run on a track it has never seen.

The state is position, heading, longitudinal speed, lateral speed, and steer angle. Lateral speed stays zero in the kinematic model, which is fair at the speeds we ran. Costs are quadratic: distance to the centerline, heading error, speed error, and control effort.

sections.heading: Making It Fast Enough
paragraphs: A useful MPPI wants on the order of a thousand trajectories. On a CPU I was at about 5 Hz, which is not a controller. The car has an NVIDIA GPU and speaks ROS from Python, so raw CUDA was the benchmark and PyTorch was the candidate. Across horizons and sample counts, PyTorch was close enough to CUDA that I stayed in PyTorch.

The first on-car runs were about 4 Hz. I locked the speed and only steered. It tended to miss the walls, and the crashes lined up with how slow the loop was. PyTorch was not actually sitting on the GPU the way I thought. A custom extension that owned the CPU/GPU copies got the loop to 21 Hz, and speed regulation started working.

More cleanup, with 1,000 trajectories and a horizon of 20 steps, got a new command at 40 Hz. The code in the repo is set up for 2,000 trajectories. My resume compresses the whole speedup as 3 Hz to 40 Hz, about 13×.

sections.heading: Seeing What the Car Was Thinking
paragraphs: I drove the car by hand with a GameCube controller, logged LiDAR, speed, and steer, and played that into the planner. LiDAR boundaries become a centerline. The drawing shows the boundary, the car, the centerline, every rollout, and the ten cheapest. That let me debug without setting up the track, and then tune the cost the same way.

sections.heading: Indoor Flight Lab, Mid-Fall 2024
paragraphs: The track was a closed loop, 1 meter wide. I started at 0.5 m/s, with a floor of 0.2 m/s so the drive servos would not chatter. At 1.5 m/s it oscillated and turned late. I cut the centerline when it went discontinuous, raised the position cost, and capped steer at ±20°. After that, 1.5 m/s was reliable. At 2 m/s on that skinny track it was not. A typical F1Tenth track is three or four times wider. I didn't get to try one.

projects.title: Ballistic missile tracking
projects.summary: Infrared tracking of a ballistic missile from a satellite constellation, with an extended Kalman filter that starts from one line of sight or from a triangulation.
projects.vizLabel: Satellite constellation and a ballistic arc between the sample launch and target.

sections.heading: What the Sim Does
paragraphs: A constellation of infrared satellites watches a missile from launch to impact. The missile trajectory is configurable. The filter's dynamics are deliberately a little wrong, because you would not know the other vehicle's model.

The repo ships three constellations: a Space-Based Infrared System case, the Space Development Agency Tranche 1 layout, and a self-made MEO design. The drawing on this page uses the custom MEO block in runSim.m: three planes, four satellites each, inclinations −60°, 0°, and +60°, semimajor axis one Earth radius plus 10,000 km. I did not unpack the saved .mat constellations, so the other two are not drawn.

The sample trajectory in missileTrajSolver.m runs from 38.89°N, 77.04°W to 55.75°N, 37.62°E. Phases are boost, midcourse, and reentry. Estimation waits until the missile is above 100 km and at least one satellite has line of sight.

sections.heading: The Filter
paragraphs: One satellite initializes along the line of sight, with a guessed range. Two or more triangulate. The time update is an RK4 step of two-body dynamics and a state transition carried to second order. The measurement is azimuth, elevation, and their rates. Angles get wrapped before the innovation so a ±π jump does not look like a huge residual.

If the missile is high but nobody can see it, the filter coasts. Under 100 km it switches to a reentry model with a guessed drag term. The script reports impact error, crossrange, and a circular error probable. I have not re-run it here, so I am not quoting those numbers.

projects.title: Planetary supply drop
projects.summary: A C++ simulation of dropping a payload from orbit onto a chosen point on Earth: orbit control, ballistic entry, a parachute, and a fuel-optimal landing.
projects.vizLabel: Schematic of orbit, entry, parachute, and powered descent.

sections.heading: Why I Started It
paragraphs: I had just finished the bachelor's and I wanted a problem that used the orbital mechanics and the vehicle dynamics together. The question was: can you drop a payload on a chosen point on Earth from a satellite? The practical answer is probably not worth the cost. It is still a good problem. I wrote the simulation in C++, prototyped algorithms in MATLAB, and drew the results in Python with VPython.

A spacecraft rides to a circular equatorial low Earth orbit. It carries its own propulsion and a capsule. The capsule enters, drops its heatshield, opens a parachute, then hands off to a lander that thrusts to the point. Propagation is RK4, except the powered-descent optimization, which uses forward Euler. Atmosphere is exponential. Gravity falls off with altitude. The launch vehicle is not part of the simulation.

sections.heading: Staying on the Reference Orbit
paragraphs: On orbit the spacecraft feels J2, drag, and solar radiation pressure. Left alone it walks off the reference. I treat the reference as the chief and the real satellite as the deputy in the Clohessy-Wiltshire frame, and I close an LQR around that linear relative motion. The gain comes from MATLAB's lqr. The command is rotated from the CW frame into ECI.

To pass over the drop latitude, the spacecraft changes inclination. The Δv is the difference between the current velocity and the velocity of the same orbit at the new inclination. When to release the capsule comes from the angle the ballistic arc covers on the Earth, plus the longitudinal phase shift between successive passes over that latitude.

sections.heading: Entry, Descent, and Landing
paragraphs: Ballistic descent propagates speed, flight-path angle, and altitude, starting from a 5° flight-path angle. Drag rotates the path until the capsule is falling straight down at chute altitude. The heatshield mass comes off, the parachute is a simple quadratic drag model, and wind is a biased random cross-range acceleration. That miss is what powered descent has to clean up.

Powered descent is G-FOLD, from the Açıkmeşe, Carson, and Blackmore paper on lossless convexification of the soft-landing problem. Two convex problems: first minimum landing error, then minimum fuel at that error or better. Constraints cover mass, thrust bounds, pointing, glideslope, and speed. Attitude is left out, on the assumption that it can be corrected faster and with less thrust. Aero is left out because the lander is slow. The C++ calls cvxpy for the solve. If it fails, the sim tells you to relax the constraints.

The C++ includes a Kalman filter for orbit determination from ground-station range and range-rate. The published simulation does not include the launch leg, or a successive-convexification version with time of flight left free.

projects.title: Drone trajectory optimization
projects.summary: Differential dynamic programming for a quadrotor, with barrier costs around obstacles, extended to receding-horizon MPC.
projects.vizLabel: Planar quadrotor flying a path that clears two obstacles.

sections.heading: The Project
paragraphs: Final project for AE 4803 in fall 2024, written with Kush Bandi. The drone dynamics are a quadrotor. The cost is a second-order approximation, and so are the dynamics, which is what makes it DDP rather than plain iLQR. Forward and backward passes repeat until the cost stops dropping. A line search scales the feedforward step.

Obstacles are barrier functions: the cost goes to infinity as the vehicle reaches the obstacle. We then wrapped the same planner in MPC so it replans during the flight. The figures below are those runs. The canvas uses the planar model from planar_quadrotor.m and flies a path around two circles. It is there so you can see the vehicle, not as a substitute for the MATLAB result.

projects.title: Thrust-vectored rockets
projects.summary: Gru and Vector, two small rockets whose motors gimbal. My first project as avionics and controls lead: a three-month build, with new members coming on while we were still designing.

sections.heading: The Vehicle
paragraphs: Active stabilization only needed a gyro, so the avionics were an IMU, a Teensy, an SD log, two servos on the gimbal, and a TeleMega to deploy the parachutes. The timeline was short, so the wiring was hand-soldered on a protoboard. Gyro samples went through a moving average.

sections.heading: Attitude and the PD Loop
paragraphs: Attitude is a quaternion from a North-East-Down world frame into the body. Launch detect comes from the accelerometer. After that, gyro increments become an instantaneous rotation quaternion and multiply onto the attitude.

I pull the angles off vertical and run a PD controller to drive them to zero. We checked the gains on the ground with the gimbal live. Pitch and yaw wanted different proportional gains because the gimbal is not equally stiff, and because of where the linkage pushes. There is no integral term. Gyro drift would wind it up.
The clip below is from November 10, 2023.

projects.title: Low-cost current transformer
projects.summary: A small current sensor for building managers who want appliance-level power. PCB in KiCad, housing in SolidWorks, about $102 a unit, with the readings sent out over the network.

sections.heading: The Sensor
paragraphs: Fall 2023, in the Energy Infrastructure and Data Engineering group at Georgia Tech's Aerospace Systems Design Laboratory. The brief was small, modular, and cheap. Georgia Tech was looking at building energy use, and the same family of sensors was planned for homes in Atlanta to compare HVAC use across neighborhoods. That is what the writeup said. I am not claiming the deployment happened.

The current transformer plugged into an audio jack, through an analog-to-digital converter, into a Particle board that posted the readings. Leaving the data on the network meant nobody had to pull an SD card.

The first PCB added a barrel jack so it could run from the wall. The housing was a square box with the antenna outside. The second pass made the board long and skinny so the antenna could live inside, and added a LiPo connector so it could run for a while with no outlet. With assembly instructions written, a unit was $102, which was the point: much cheaper than the commercial sensors, and it already reported online.
My resume also says the current-sensor software ran on a Raspberry Pi. I am leaving both notes here rather than collapsing them into one architecture.

paragraphs: QuadGNC is a collection of in-house GNC, simulation, and flight-software code for a quadcopter. That is the whole public description, so this page stops there.
